extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readership (readers interested in wartime events and legal proceedings)
extracted.subtask_description: News reporting about the planning, legal standards, and proceedings of war-crimes trials (Pacific theatre), including procedural safeguards, jurisdictional questions, scope of prosecution, and sentencing. Focused on how trials are to be conducted and reported to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trials to be free and open
rubrics_metrics.description: Keenan said trials probably would be free and open; the accused would be given fair notice of charges against them so that they do not think they committed any crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlining preliminary plans for the trials—which will involve more than 250 war crimes suspects—Keenan said trials probably would be free and open. Speaking at a 30-minute press conference after a lengthy session, Keenan said that the groups of defendants would be tried in groups and that the accused would be given fair notice of charges against them so that they do not think they committed any crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused are to be 'presumed innocent until proved guilty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explicitly states the principle: 'the accused presumed innocent until proved guilty.' This is cited as part of how the trials should be conducted and presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trials to be concluded rapidly
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials should be concluded 'as rapidly as possible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keenan emphasized the requirement that trials be concluded as rapidly as possible, and that the U.S. would not indulge 'a Roman holiday for technicalities either by the prosecution or defense.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping of defendants by broad time periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspects will be tried in groups built around broad time periods in which they were active; groups of defendants would be formed by major time periods going back to July 1937.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like their German counterparts, Japanese war crimes suspects will be tried in groups. Keenan said the groups of defendants would be built around broad time periods in which they were active. They will go back to July 1937, when the China war started.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect rights of other nations / avoid highhanded attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial preparations and procedures should respect the rights of other nations and show that the United States is not taking a highhanded attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keenan said trial preparations were to respect the rights of other nations and to show that the United States was not taking a highhanded attitude, reflecting sensitivity to international perceptions while prosecuting war crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of prosecutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution's temporal scope may extend back to July 1937 (start of the China war) and will cover defined periods of activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keenan stated that the trials would go back to July 1937, indicating an explicit decision on the period to be covered by prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military commissions' jurisdiction over wartime offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A military commission has the right to try enemy belligerents for violations of the law of war committed prior to their capture even after cessation of hostilities and when the civil courts are open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reply to jurisdictional challenges, McGrath argued that by long recognized procedure of the law of war, a military commission may try enemy belligerents for law-of-war violations committed prior to capture, even after hostilities cease and civil courts are functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charges must state offenses against the law of war
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal charge must state offenses against the law of war, e.g., that the accused 'permitted members of his command to commit brutal atrocities and other high crimes against nationals of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Justice Department's brief asserted that 'the charge against Yamashita does state offenses against the law in war,' quoting language that the commander permitted members of his command to commit brutal atrocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command responsibility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A commander may be held responsible if he 'failed to provide effective control of your troops' and thereby permitted atrocities under his command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commission found that atrocities 'were not sporadic incidents, but were often methodically supervised by Japanese commissioned officers' and that Yamashita 'failed to provide effective control of your troops' as required by circumstances, forming the basis for conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentencing concurrence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A death sentence by the commission requires concurrence by two-thirds or more of the commission members (secret ballot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes: 'secret ballot, two-thirds or more of this commission concurring, this commission finds you guilty as charged and sentences you to death by hanging.' This sets the internal voting threshold for capital sentencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of appeal and review channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings and sentences by a military commission are subject to review by higher military authorities (e.g., commander of army forces in the Western Pacific, General MacArthur) and may be the subject of petitions to civilian courts (e.g., U.S. Supreme Court) on jurisdictional grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yamashita's execution 'must await review of the commission's findings by the commander of army forces in the Western Pacific and confirmation by General MacArthur.' The article also notes an appeal on jurisdictional grounds pending with the U.S. Supreme Court and other internal military review options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair procedure / avoidance of excessive technicalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials should be fair but not bogged down by excessive technicalities; 'this is not to be a Roman holiday for technicalities either by the prosecution or defense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keenan remarked that trials would not be prolonged and should avoid becoming a 'Roman holiday for technicalities,' indicating a standard balancing due process with efficient prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for other nations in indictments and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecutors should respect international concerns when indicting and conducting trials, avoiding unilateral or insensitive actions toward other interested powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports that an international court seems likely 'since other interested powers have been asked,' and Keenan emphasized respecting the rights of other nations in trial procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of defendants to include top government, military and industrial leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of suspects and trial targets includes cabinet members, army, navy officers, industrial leaders, and top officials; prosecutions aim at leaders who 'set in motion the plans' rather than only those who executed orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keenan and others outlined that groups would include 'cabinet members, army, navy officers and industrial leaders' and that the focus may be on those who conceived and planned rather than those who merely executed the acts (e.g., 'it is not the men who dropped the bombs but the men who set in motion the plans').
